title: Glass ionomer & compomer
blurb: The fluoride-releasing, chemically bonding materials: conventional glass ionomer, resin-modified glass ionomer and compomer, and when each is used.
question: A 7-year-old with several cavities needs a filling in a deciduous molar, and the dentist asks for a material that bonds to the tooth and releases fluoride. You hand-mix it, but by the time the dentist is ready it looks dull and grainy. Which material is it, and why might it now fail?

teach.body: Glass ionomer cement (GIC) is a tooth-coloured material made from a fluoride-containing glass powder and a liquid of polyacrylic acid. When they are mixed, the acid attacks the glass and the material sets by an acid-base reaction. No light is needed. Two properties make GIC special: it bonds chemically to enamel and dentine, and it releases fluoride into the surrounding tooth for a long time, helping to prevent decay around the filling.

items.label: Releases fluoride, and can take up more from toothpaste
Chemical (ionic) bond to enamel and dentine
Thermal expansion close to natural tooth
Biocompatible and gentle on the pulp

teach.caption: Its weak points: lower strength and wear resistance than amalgam or composite, and a more opaque, less lifelike appearance.

rows.label: Cervical (Class V) cavities from abrasion, erosion or root caries
Fillings in deciduous teeth and for high caries-risk patients
Lining or base under amalgam or composite
Cementing crowns, bridges and orthodontic bands
Interim fillings to stabilise decay before definitive treatment

teach.note: A conventional GIC liner is a good choice under amalgam when the dentist wants fluoride release.

teach.h: A classic GIC site: cervical lesions
teach.caption: Charted as you face the patient. Class V cavities sit at the neck of the tooth (here the labial and buccal cervical areas), often on root surface where there is little enamel to etch. GIC's chemical bond to dentine and its fluoride release suit them well.

steps.label: Condition the tooth
steps.sub: Mild polyacrylic acid conditioner if the dentist uses one, then rinse

steps.label: Dispense correctly
steps.sub: Exact powder:liquid ratio, or activate the capsule

steps.label: Mix quickly
steps.sub: Hand-mix on a pad, or triturate the capsule in the amalgamator

steps.label: Place while glossy
steps.sub: A shiny surface means it can still bond

steps.label: Protect the surface
steps.sub: Varnish or bonding resin while it matures

teach.caption: Early on, GIC is spoiled both by moisture (saliva washes it out) and by drying out (it cracks and crazes). That's why the surface is protected.

teach.body: A good GIC mix is smooth and glossy. The gloss shows that unreacted acid is still free to bond with the tooth. If the mix is dull, grainy and setting before it is placed, too much powder was used or mixing was too slow or started too early. That mix will not bond well and should be discarded and remixed. Encapsulated GIC avoids most ratio problems: activate the capsule, triturate it for the stated time and place it straight away with the applicator gun.

bands.label: Acid-base set; most fluoride; chemical bond
GIC plus resin; acid-base + light cure
Mainly resin; light cure; needs bonding agent
Resin; light cure; best looks and strength

teach.caption: Moving towards composite: more resin, better strength and appearance, but less fluoride release and less chemical bonding.
RMGIC (resin-modified glass ionomer) can be set on command with the curing light. Compomer is a polyacid-modified composite: it handles like composite and comes in compules.

teach.text: Compomer is NOT a type of glass ionomer that bonds chemically: it is mostly resin, so it needs a bonding agent and a curing light. If a question says 'bonds chemically and releases the most fluoride', the answer is conventional glass ionomer.

items: GIC = fluoride glass powder + polyacrylic acid; sets by an acid-base reaction.
Bonds chemically to enamel and dentine and releases fluoride over time.
Correct ratio and quick mixing; place while glossy. Dull and grainy = discard.
Protect from moisture and drying while it sets.
RMGIC adds resin and light-curing; compomer is mainly resin and needs a bonding agent.

summary: You can now explain how glass ionomer sets and bonds, why its fluoride release makes it the choice for cervical cavities, deciduous teeth, high caries-risk patients and linings, handle and judge a GIC mix, and tell conventional GIC, resin-modified GIC and compomer apart.

A.q: A freshly mixed glass ionomer looks dull, grainy and is setting before it can be placed. What is the most likely cause?
options: Wrong powder:liquid ratio or slow mixing
The matrix band was placed before mixing
A clean plastic spatula was used
A.why: Too much powder or delayed mixing shortens working time and gives a dull, grainy mix that won't bond well.

whyNot.0: Shade has no effect on how the material handles or sets.
whyNot.2: Matrix placement doesn't affect the mix itself.
whyNot.3: A clean plastic spatula is appropriate for mixing and isn't a cause.

A.q: Which property of glass ionomer makes it a good choice for patients at high risk of decay?
A.why: GIC releases fluoride into the surrounding tooth, helping to prevent decay around the restoration.

whyNot.0: GIC is fairly opaque; translucency is a strength of composite.
whyNot.1: GIC wears faster than amalgam or composite.
whyNot.2: GIC is not a metal and is weaker than amalgam.

A.q: How does conventional glass ionomer set?
options: By an acid-base reaction after mixing
When exposed to blue light from the curing lamp
By losing water to the air
By heat from the patient's mouth
A.why: The polyacrylic acid reacts with the glass powder in an acid-base setting reaction; no light is needed.

whyNot.1: Light curing applies to composite, compomer and the resin part of RMGIC.
whyNot.2: Drying out actually damages setting GIC, causing cracks.
whyNot.3: Body heat speeds most reactions slightly but isn't the setting mechanism.

B.q: The dentist wants a lining under a deep amalgam and would like fluoride release. Which material is most suitable?
B.why: Conventional GIC bonds chemically to dentine, insulates and releases fluoride, making it a good liner under amalgam.

whyNot.0: ZOE is sedative but doesn't release fluoride.
whyNot.2: Addition silicone is an impression material, not a liner.
whyNot.3: Flowable composite releases little or no fluoride and needs etching and bonding.

B.q: Why is the surface of a newly placed glass ionomer often coated with varnish or bonding resin?
options: To make it set under the blue curing light
To lighten its final shade to match
To protect it from moisture and drying
To stop fluoride escaping from it
B.why: While GIC is maturing, saliva can wash it out and drying makes it crack, so the surface is protected.

whyNot.0: Conventional GIC doesn't need light to set.
whyNot.1: The coating protects the surface; it isn't used to alter shade.
whyNot.3: Fluoride release is a benefit; the coating isn't there to stop it.

B.q: Which material is a polyacid-modified composite that needs a bonding agent and a curing light?
B.why: Compomer is mostly resin with some glass ionomer components. It is light-cured and used with a bonding agent.

whyNot.0: Conventional GIC bonds chemically and sets without light.
whyNot.1: Zinc polycarboxylate is a cement that bonds chemically, without light.
whyNot.2: Calcium hydroxide is a lining material, not a restorative.

C.q: Which type of cavity is glass ionomer especially suited to?
options: Incisal edge fracture of a front tooth
Large core build-up under heavy bite
C.why: Cervical (Class V) lesions are low-load areas with little enamel. GIC bonds to dentine and releases fluoride there.

whyNot.0: Large load-bearing posterior cavities need a stronger material such as amalgam or composite.
whyNot.1: Incisal edges need strength and good appearance, which composite provides better.
whyNot.2: Conventional GIC is too weak for a large build-up under heavy biting load.

C.q: What does a glossy surface on a freshly mixed glass ionomer show?
options: It still has free acid to bond
C.why: Gloss shows unreacted acid is still present, so the material can still bond chemically to the tooth.

whyNot.1: A fully set GIC loses its gloss; glossy means it is still workable.
whyNot.2: The correct ratio gives a glossy mix; gloss is the sign of a good mix.

C.q: Which statement about resin-modified glass ionomer (RMGIC) is correct?
options: It releases no fluoride once it has set
It sets only by light curing
It is set by acid-base and light
It must be mixed with mercury
C.why: RMGIC has a dual set: the glass ionomer acid-base reaction plus light-curing of its resin component.

whyNot.0: RMGIC still releases fluoride, much like conventional GIC.
whyNot.1: The acid-base reaction continues even without light.
whyNot.3: Mercury is only used in amalgam.

reteach.title: Think of GIC as a slow-release fluoride sponge
reteach.question: Imagine a sponge that sticks to the tooth on its own and slowly leaks fluoride for years. What would it be best for, and what would its weaknesses be?

blocks.h: Sticky, protective, but not the toughest
blocks.body: GIC grabs hold of enamel and dentine chemically, so it doesn't need etching or undercuts. Like a sponge, it keeps releasing fluoride and can soak more up from toothpaste. That makes it ideal where decay risk is high or enamel is thin: baby teeth, cervical cavities and linings. But a sponge isn't the hardest material, so GIC isn't chosen for big fillings that take heavy biting forces.

blocks.text: A dull, grainy GIC mix has lost its ability to bond. Don't hand it over: tell the dentist and remix.

explain.body: GIC is a fluoride-containing glass powder mixed with polyacrylic acid. It sets by an acid-base reaction and bonds chemically (ionically) to the calcium in enamel and dentine.

test.q: What is the liquid in a conventional glass ionomer cement?
test.why: GIC liquid is polyacrylic acid, which reacts with the fluoride glass powder.

whyNot.0: Phosphoric acid is the liquid of zinc phosphate and the acid in etchant.
whyNot.1: Eugenol is the liquid in zinc oxide eugenol.
whyNot.3: Mercury is used only in amalgam.

explain.body: GIC releases fluoride for a long time and can recharge from toothpaste. It is used for cervical cavities, deciduous teeth, high caries-risk patients, linings and bases, luting and interim fillings.

test.q: A patient has several cervical abrasion cavities and a high caries risk. Which material property makes GIC suitable?
test.why: GIC's fluoride release helps protect the surrounding tooth, and it bonds to dentine at the cervical margin.

whyNot.1: GIC is more opaque than composite.
whyNot.2: GIC is not metallic and is weaker than amalgam.
whyNot.3: GIC still needs good moisture control, especially while setting.

explain.body: Use the exact powder:liquid ratio, mix quickly, and place while the mix is glossy. Dull and grainy means too much powder or slow mixing, and it won't bond. Protect the surface from saliva and drying.

test.q: What should you do with a GIC mix that has gone dull and grainy before use?
test.why: A dull, grainy mix has lost the free acid needed to bond, so it is discarded and a fresh mix made.

whyNot.0: Adding liquid to a setting mix ruins its properties.
whyNot.2: It won't bond properly however quickly it is placed.
whyNot.3: Heat would speed setting, making it worse.

explain.body: RMGIC is GIC with added resin: it sets by acid-base reaction and light, is stronger and less moisture-sensitive early on, and still releases fluoride. Compomer is mostly composite resin: light-cured, needs a bonding agent and releases less fluoride.

test.q: Which material needs a bonding agent because it is mostly resin?
test.why: Compomer is a polyacid-modified composite, so like composite it needs a bonding agent.

whyNot.0: Conventional GIC bonds chemically without a bonding agent.
whyNot.1: RMGIC still bonds chemically through its glass ionomer reaction.
whyNot.3: Polycarboxylate cement bonds chemically to tooth.
